summary: Defines a general set of parameters that describe the characteristics of network elements and are used to control them in the IETF integrated services framework. Different services can then share the same parameter definitions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2215 gives routers that support quality of service reservations a shared set of numbers for describing what they can do on a path: how much bandwidth is free, how much delay they add, the largest packet that fits, and whether the path is fully managed. Each router reports its own value, and a rule fixed per parameter combines those values along the path, so a sender learns what the whole path can carry before it asks for a reservation.

subtitle: The shared set of numbers every Integrated Services router reports about itself, and how they add up along a path.

tldr.problem: An application that wants a quality of service reservation needs to know what the path can actually do: how much bandwidth is free, how much delay each hop adds, how large a packet fits, and whether every router on the way really takes part in reservations.
tldr.mechanism: This memo defines a shared set of general parameters. Every network element reports a local value for each one, and a composition rule fixed per parameter combines those local values along the path into one value the endpoint can read.
tldr.outcome: The memo gives each parameter a number, fixes the ranges the wire format must cover, and reserves a value for 'I cannot tell'. Individual QoS control services, such as Guaranteed Service and Controlled-load Service, refer to these definitions, so one router describes itself the same way to every service.

today: RFC 2215 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It remains the shared definition of the general Integrated Services parameters that the individual QoS control service specifications refer to, among them RFC 2212 for Guaranteed Service and RFC 2211 for Controlled-load Service.

sections.title: What the Memo Defines
sections.content:
RFC 2215 defines the general control and characterization parameters used by network elements that support the IETF integrated services framework for quality of service (QoS) control. A parameter is general when it has one definition and one shared meaning across all QoS control services, so several services can reuse the same number instead of each inventing its own.

The memo separates two kinds of parameter. Control parameters carry information from an application to the network about a QoS request; the traffic specification (TSpec) produced by a sending or receiving application is the example given. Characterization parameters describe the management environment along the path of a flow that is asking for active end-to-end QoS control, for example which QoS control services are available along the path and how much bandwidth the path has.

Every characterization parameter has a local value, which describes one network element, and a composed value, the running result of combining local values along the path. The parameter definition fixes the composition rule that says how an incoming composed value and the local value are combined into a new composed value, which is then passed to the next element. Composition may proceed downstream towards the receiver or upstream towards the sender.

Because these parameters describe a specific path, they are conceptually per next hop rather than per interface or per element. An element sitting at the edge of a shared medium may have to report different values for different next hops inside that medium, and a vendor may choose to publish a documented tolerance range so that one value can stand for all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo gives every router that supports quality of service reservations the same set of numbers for describing itself, so different services can share them. Each router reports a local value, and a rule fixed per parameter combines those values along the path into a single value.

sections.title: Parameter Identifiers
sections.content:
Parameters are given machine-oriented identifiers using the method described in RFC 2216. Each identifier pairs a service_number, which names the QoS control service the parameter belongs to, with a parameter_number, which names the parameter itself. The memo writes such a pair in the textual form <service_number, parameter_number>.

Because the parameters defined here are common to every QoS control service, their parameter_number values are taken from the general range, 1 to 127. Numbers from 128 to 254 name parameters whose definitions are specific to one service, and for those both numbers are needed to know what the parameter means.

Service number 1 is reserved for the default value described in the next section. Service numbers 2 through 254 are allocated to individual QoS control services: Guaranteed Service has number 2 and Controlled-load Service has number 5.

The ranges are chosen so that the identifier can form the tail portion of a MIB object identifier, which makes the values easy to publish to network management applications. The identifiers travel inside protocol messages, such as the RSVP setup messages described in RFC 2210, or inside management interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parameter gets a two-part number: one part names the service, the other names the parameter. Because the parameters in this memo mean the same thing for every service, they use the low number range, 1 to 127, and the service part says 'applies to all services' with the number 1.

sections.title: Default and Service-Specific Values
sections.content:
Frequently the same value of a general parameter is correct for every QoS control service a node offers. Such a value is called a default or global value, and the node exports one number that applies to all its services instead of a separate copy per service. In the common case this reduces both the size of setup messages and the work of processing them.

Sometimes one service needs a different value. The memo's example: a router whose Guaranteed Service implementation is limited by its scheduler or hardware to a maximum packet size smaller than the router's best-effort path can export a service-specific PATH_MTU. The router might then publish 1500 as the default PATH_MTU and 250 as the PATH_MTU that applies to Guaranteed Service. A service-specific value is also called an override value, because it overrides the default for the service it names.

The identifier carries this distinction. A value with the identifier <1, parameter_number> is a default value that applies to all services unless a service-specific value for the same parameter overrides it. A value whose service_number is not 1 is a service-specific value and applies only to that service.

The memo then gives the composition procedure in six steps. The arriving value, the local value and the result are the three inputs. The steps are: if the arriving value belongs to a parameter specific to one service, compose it with the local value of that service; if the arriving value is service-specific for a generally defined parameter and the local implementation of that service exports its own service-specific value, compose the two service-specific values; if the local implementation does not export one, compose the arriving service-specific value with the local global value and pass the result as service-specific; if the arriving value is global and any local service exports a service-specific value, compose the arriving global value with each of those service-specific values and pass each result as a service-specific value, adding a field to the message for each; and if the arriving value is global, compose it with the local global value and pass the result on as a global value.

The basic rule behind all six steps is simple: use the service-specific value if one exists, and the global value otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Most routers report one number per parameter that applies to all services. A service that needs a different number, such as a smaller maximum packet size, reports its own value, and that value wins for that service alone. The memo lists the exact steps a router follows to combine the value it received with the value it holds.

sections.title: The General Parameters
sections.content:
Section 3 defines each general parameter. Five of them are characterization parameters, with a local value, a composed value and a composition rule.

NON-IS_HOP reports whether the path is fully managed. The local value is 1 if the element does not implement the relevant QoS control service, or knows there is a break in the chain of elements that do, and 0 otherwise. The composition rule is the logical OR, so a composed value of 1 at the end of a path means at least one point along it does not offer the service. A router that sends packets into an IP tunnel must assume the tunneled packets get no QoS control unless it or the setup protocol can prove otherwise. When the global flag is set, the receiver should treat all other parameter values on that path as possibly inaccurate. The parameter may be represented in any form that expresses true and false, but the representation must allow the value to be read and set even when the element cannot otherwise parse the message, because an element that does not support the service cannot know to set the flag. The RSVP message format of RFC 2210 carries this parameter as a single-bit flag, called the break bit.

NUMBER_OF_IS_HOPS counts the integrated-services-aware elements on the path. IS stands for integrated services aware: an element that conforms to the requirements of this and the other referenced documents, need not offer a specific service, but if it does it must support and characterize that service, and if it does not it must set the NON-IS_HOP flag for that service. The composition rule increments the counter by one at each aware hop, and the composed value ranges from 1 to 255, limited by the bound on the IP hop count.

AVAILABLE_PATH_BANDWIDTH is an estimate of the bandwidth the element has available for packets following the path, taking into account administrative and policy controls as well as physical resources. The composition rule is the minimum, so the composed value reports the smallest bandwidth on the path. Values are measured in bytes per second and the representation must express anything from 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second, about what is believed to be the maximum theoretical bandwidth of a single strand of fiber. A floating point representation accurate to at least 0.1% is encouraged, and negative numbers, infinities and NANs are not allowed. Because the value has to be published before any specific QoS request exists, it is often hard to be accurate, and overestimating by a significant amount is acceptable. A local value of zero means the element cannot estimate the bandwidth, so a composed value of zero means the real bandwidth is unknown.

MINIMUM_PATH_LATENCY is the smallest packet delay the element adds, from propagation and from processing limits, but not including any variable queuing delay. The composition rule is summation with a clamp of 2 to the power of 32 minus 1 on the maximum value. Latencies are reported in units of one microsecond; an individual element can advertise a value between 1 and 2 to the power of 28, somewhat over two minutes, and the total can reach 2 to the power of 32 minus 2. The distinguished value 2 to the power of 32 minus 1 means indeterminate latency, and a network element that cannot predict its latency sets its local value to it. A conforming element is free to measure loosely, but must be accurate to the nearest 100 microsecond granularity, and measuring in milliseconds is not acceptable. Together with the queuing delay bound offered by services such as Guaranteed Service, this parameter gives an application both the minimum and the maximum delivery delay, which is what it needs to size a de-jitter buffer.

PATH_MTU is the maximum transmission unit for packets following the path, defined as the largest unit the element can take without fragmentation, counting IP and upper layer headers but not link level headers. The composition rule is the minimum, so the composed value is the largest packet that can cross the whole path without fragmentation. Every integrated-services-aware element must provide a correct and valid value for it. A service module may override it with a smaller MTU but may not specify one larger than the global value. Values are measured in bytes, and the representation must express anything from 1 byte to 2 to the power of 32 minus 1 bytes. Existing MTU discovery mechanisms cannot be used, because they inform only the sender and do not let a QoS control service specify an MTU smaller than the physical one.

All of these parameters are mandatory in the sense that a network element claiming to support integrated services must recognize arriving values, process them correctly and export a reasonable value in response. For some parameters the specification requires an accurate local value; for others it is enough to signal the reserved indeterminate value.
sections.plainLanguage: Five numbers describe a path. One says whether every router on it takes part in reservations. One counts the routers that do. One estimates the free bandwidth, and the path's value is the smallest estimate along it. One gives the smallest delay a router adds, and the path's value is the sum. One gives the largest packet that fits, and the path's value is the smallest of those too.

sections.title: The Token Bucket Traffic Specification
sections.content:
The sixth definition in Section 3, TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC, is not a characterization parameter. Intermediate nodes inside the network do not export local values for it. It is included here as a data structure definition because the same traffic description may be used by more than one QoS control service, and it is assigned parameter number 127.

It describes a flow with a simple token bucket filter plus three more values. The token bucket part holds an average or token rate [r] and a bucket depth [b], and both must be positive. The token rate is measured in bytes of IP datagrams per second and ranges from 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second. The bucket depth is measured in bytes and ranges from 1 byte to 250 gigabytes. A floating point representation accurate to at least 0.1% is encouraged for both. The peak traffic rate [p] is also measured in bytes of IP datagrams per second, ranges from 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second, and may be set to positive infinity to mean unknown or unspecified.

The minimum policed unit [m] is a whole number of bytes covering the application data and all protocol headers at or above the IP level, such as IP, TCP, UDP and RTP, but not the link level header, because those headers change size as the packet crosses different parts of the network. Every datagram smaller than [m] is treated as being of size [m] for resource allocation and policing. That lets the network estimate the per-packet resources a flow needs, since the maximum packet rate can be computed from [b] and [m], and it bounds the bandwidth the flow's link level headers consume by the ratio of the link level header size to [m]. Without [m] the network would have to assume every flow always sent minimum sized packets, which the memo calls unacceptable.

The maximum packet size [M] is the biggest packet that conforms to the traffic specification, also measured in bytes. Packets larger than it may not receive QoS-controlled service, because they are considered not to meet the specification. Both [m] and [M] must be positive, and [m] must be less than or equal to [M].

Each parameter definition also carries an XDR description, the external data representation standard of RFC 1832, giving an appropriate wire form for the values. The dual definition of a minimal set of properties plus a wire description is meant to encourage a common representation while still allowing others where the circumstances require, such as ASN.1 inside SNMP. The setup messages of RFC 2210 use the XDR representation.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo also fixes one shared structure for describing a flow's traffic, because several services need it. It holds an average rate, a bucket depth, a peak rate, a smallest packet size to charge the flow for, and a largest packet size the flow may send.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says that implementing the characterization parameters creates no known new avenues for malicious attack on the network infrastructure. It does note that implementing them reveals some additional information about a network's performance, which in extremely rare circumstances could be viewed as a security matter by the network provider.

The accuracy rules elsewhere in the memo are the practical limit on how much is revealed. An element that cannot compute a value exports the reserved indeterminate value, and an element that cannot estimate the available bandwidth exports zero, which the receiver must read as unknown. The NON-IS_HOP flag deliberately hides the reason for a gap: the element sets it when it does not fully understand the arriving message, and it must be readable even then.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says these parameters open no new attack route. The one concern it notes is that a router now publishes a little about its own performance, which a network operator may occasionally treat as sensitive.

items.label: NON_IS_HOP, local
items.desc: 1 when this element does not implement the relevant QoS control service, or knows the chain is broken; 0 otherwise.

items.label: NON_IS_HOP, composed
items.desc: Logical OR of the local values along the path. Set means at least one element on the path does not offer the service.

items.label: NUMBER_OF_IS_HOPS, local
items.desc: Assigned by an element that conforms to the integrated services requirements.

items.label: NUMBER_OF_IS_HOPS, composed
items.desc: Count of integrated-services-aware elements traversed, from 1 to 255.

items.label: AVAILABLE_PATH_BANDWIDTH, local
items.desc: Estimate of the bandwidth available for packets following the path, in bytes per second.

items.label: AVAILABLE_PATH_BANDWIDTH, composed
items.desc: The smallest bandwidth on the path: the minimum of the local value and the arriving composed value.

items.label: MINIMUM_PATH_LATENCY, local
items.desc: The smallest packet delay this element adds, in microseconds.

items.label: MINIMUM_PATH_LATENCY, composed
items.desc: The sum of the local delays along the path, clamped at 2 to the power of 32 minus 1.

items.label: PATH_MTU, local
items.desc: The largest IP packet this element handles without fragmentation, in bytes.

items.label: PATH_MTU, composed
items.desc: The smallest MTU on the path: the minimum of the local value and the arriving composed value.

items.label: TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC
items.desc: Traffic specification in token bucket form. Not a characterization parameter: intermediate elements export no local value for it.
